maintopic: TRAVELLING EXPENSES OF MEMBERS BETWEEN RESIDENCE AND OTTAWA
TRAVELLING EXPENSES OF MEMBERS BETWEEN RESIDENCE AND OTTAWA
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) stated on the floor of the house on Monday last that the chief treasury officer who performs the duties of accountant of the house had refused to pay his travelling expenses by air and also those of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson). He said:
I request that Your Honour give the reason which you gave to the accountant of the House of Commons as to why the expense accounts for the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and myself were refused.
This was the first time I heard there was any trouble in connection with these expense accounts; but I took no exception to the hon. member speaking on this matter at the time because he started by saying he rose to a question of privilege. By the time he was through I saw that the main object of his statement was a complaint against a part of the house's administration which is under my control. I then said:
I call the attention of the hon. member to a very well known rule, that the Speaker should not be questioned from the floor of the house.
I nevertheless assured the hon. member that due consideration would be given his remarks.
It is a well known rule laid down in May's 14th edition, page 334, that:
Questions dealing with matters within the jurisdiction of the Speaker should be addressed to the Speaker by private notice.
Payment of members' travelling expenses has always been under the control of the commissioners of the internal economy of the house, who, for the present session, are the hon. ministers of Justice, External Affairs, Finance and Fisheries. Section 16 of the House of Commons Act provides that those hon. ministers shall act together with the Speaker, and section 18 of the act says:
All sums of money voted upon such estimates (the estimates of the house), or payable to members of the House of Commons under the Senate and House of Commons Act shall be subject to the order of the commissioners, or any three of them, of whom the Speaker shall be one.
The commissioners have often considered the members' travelling expenses but they have not yet discussed the advisability of applying section 43 (1) of the Senate and House of Commons Act to travel by air. A meeting of the commissioners was called two weeks ago and had to be postponed because ministers were too busy attending other official business. I will make it a point to submit to them the cases of the hon. members for Vancouver North and Comox-Alberni, which in my opinion deserve the most serious consideration.

maintopic: TRAVELLING EXPENSES OF MEMBERS BETWEEN RESIDENCE AND OTTAWA

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the statement Your Honour has just made I note that the hon. member for Vancouver North in making his statement said this:
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) informs me that he regularly travels by air and his accounts are approved.
I know the hon. member does not wish to misrepresent me, but he must have misunderstood me. I did not want him to understand that I regularly travel by air and that my accounts were paid. Occasionally when the adjournment of the house was so short that all of my time in going from my home and returning would be spent in travel, I have travelled by air and presented the accounts to the accountant of the house, with vouchers, and they have been paid. But that was not done on more than two or three occasions, and it is not the regular procedure.

speechtext:
1.	What disposition is made of the unemployment insurance fund?
2.	Are these moneys deposited with the chartered banks?
3.	Is any of this money invested and if so, what investments are involved?
4.	Is any of this money used for any purpose other than benefits and administration of the act and if so, for what purposes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PERSONNEL IN VARIOUS COUNTRIES-MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
1.	The unemployment insurance fund is used for the payment of unemployment insurance benefits and any moneys in excess of the current requirements for that purpose are invested in dominion government securities.
2.	Moneys received as contributions to the unemployment insurance fund are not deposited with the chartered banks. However, deposits of funds from the unemployment insurance fund are maintained in certain chartered banks throughout the country to redeem benefit warrants issued in the payment of unemployment insurance benefits and to facilitate the payment of these benefits by cash vouchers in certain designated offices.
3.	All moneys in the unemployment insurance fund over and above the immediate requirements for the payment of unemployment insurance benefits are invested in securities of the government of Canada.
4.	The wording of this question is actually not in accordance with the conditions in that no money is taken from the unemployment insurance fund to cover the cost of administering the act. The only purposes, other than for the payment of unemployment insurance benefits, for which these funds are used are to provide for the refunds of contributions made in error to the fund and to provide expenses in connection with the pledging of securities or advances to the fund as outlined in section 79 of the act.

speechtext: I wish to reply to a question asked at the last sitting by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). It concerns veterans occupying some four hundred housing units in Ville St. Laurent in Montreal. I might point out that this is not a veterans project. It was built during the war to house munitions workers, and if there are any veterans in the project they have moved in to occupy the vacancies which have occurred since the war.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ULTIMATUM GIVEN TO VETERANS AT VILLE ST. LAURENT
speechtext: There is a large number of them there now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ULTIMATUM GIVEN TO VETERANS AT VILLE ST. LAURENT
speechtext:
The number is not very large. I have the number. There are not many.
On June 13 last an agreement was reached with the municipal officials concerned that the four hundred wartime housing units situated partly in Montreal and partly in Ville St. Laurent, and known as the Cartierville project, would be made available for sale to tenants. Prices ranging from $2,900 to $3,725, depending upon the size of the housing unit, were then established by the corporation. These prices include the cost of permanent concrete foundations which will be installed after sale.
The terms of sale are adjusted so that the monthly purchase instalment approximates the monthly rental that he has been paying. To date, sixty-two sales to tenants have been made or are in the process of completion.
It has been suggested that tenants have been told that unless they buy the houses they will be forced to vacate. This is not quite the case. If the tenant is unwilling to purchase the house, he may remain as a tenant, either in that particular house or in another house in the same project. In some cases, individuals in the project are anxious to buy certain houses, and exchanges are effected to look after the wishes of the purchaser by offering comparable accommodation to the tenant.
A committee of the tenants of the Cartierville project is today meeting with officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Montreal.

I do not think that in Canada three of our major groups-farmers, millers and grain handling firms should be at the mercy of a bunch of speculators on the Winnipeg grain exchange. He said that they have seats on the exchange, and have their men on the floor. That is perfectly true.
Co-operatives in western Canada, operating under our present system, must of necessity use the Winnipeg grain exchange, either themselves or through the medium of a commission firm. It is much more intelligent for them to use their own people on the exchange than to have commission firms doing their business for them. But the hon. member for Calgary West did not say that the men who have headed those organizations for twenty-five years, who came up through farm organizations-first through their local pool committees, then as delegates and then as	directors-were
unanimous in saying that to use the Winnipeg grain exchange was not the best manner in which to handle our western grain.
I like the hon. member for Calgary West. He admitted that his only experience with the "Winnipeg grain exchange was when a few years ago he took a flier on the exchange and lost a couple of thousand dollars. Yet the hon. member advised the house that we should [DOT]continue the Winnipeg grain exchange. I would rather take the advice of the directors of our pools who have had twenty-five years' experience, who have bought and sold many millions of bushels on the exchange, and who are satisfied that it is not necessary for the successful marketing of our western grain.
I say we should close the Winnipeg grain exchange, and that our grain should be marketed through the wheat, board. If our coarse grains are to be marketed through some organization, then that organization should be either the wheat board or some other board set up by the government to do for coarse grains what the wheat board is doing for wheat.

I should deal for a few moments with the question of seed grains. I am receiving letters from the west stating that there is a shortage of seed grain in western Canada-I am referring to registered and certified seed. There was more confusion last November in western Canada in connection with seed grains than there was over the matter of coarse grains-at least that was the condition in the part of the west in which I live, where we produce perhaps the greatest amount of seed grain.
We had been exporting our seed grain during 1946 under quota permits. In November the method of exporting under quota permits was changed to a blanket quota system whereby our exports of seed grain were increased tremendously. Some time in August we found in western Canada that the seed grain handling firms out there were sending men through the province in an effort to get contracts with farmers who were growing certified and registered seed. Apparently these men who were sent out had a list of names of all the certified and registered seed producers in western Canada. The result was that a tremendous amount of seed grain in western Canada was signed up under contracts at a price of approximately $2 a bushel. The farmers did not know at that time that the wheat contract price for 1948 was going to be $2 a bushel. They did not have the information the government had that there was going to be a tremendous demand from Europe for seed grain, a demand which was out of all proportion to demands in other years. For instance, I believe Switzerland placed an order in Canada for 10,000 metric tons of seed wheat, something that was unheard of formerly because Switzerland normally sows fall wheat. But because of conditions over there, they found that their fall wheat crop was a failure and that this year they were going to have to sow spring wheat, with the result that they placed orders in Canada.
I do not know whether these seed firms had prior information on this matter, but I do know it was mighty strange that these people proceeded to divide up western Canada and went out to get contracts from the farmers. As I said, they succeeded in getting contracts for hundreds of thousands of bushels of our certified seed wheat at about $2 a bushel.

I said at the beginning that the farmers were alarmed at the rising costs of production. Today three things largely determine the cost of production of agricultural products. These are farm machinery, gas and oil, and fertilizer. They are the three largest items that enter into our cost of production.
We have had a lot of talk about prices of farm machinery. A committee of this house inquired into farm machinery prices in 1937. I have here the evidence taken and the committee's recommendations and I may say that this is why we were suspicious of the effectiveness of the present committee inquiring into prices. We wonder if we shall not get the same results that we got from the farm machinery inquiry. That committee did at least make recommendations; the present prices committee cannot even go that far. I wish to quote a few of the recommendations of the committee on farm implement prices:
(4) That the companies engaged in the industry, over the period of their operations as a whole, have made substantial profits on the capital invested in each company.

I intend to do so, though knowing it will be embarrassing to him. Mr. Pratt was born at North Gower, Ontario, on September 13, 1896. He completed four years at high school before reaching the age of sixteen years. After attending classes which were equivalent of one year's university training, he first entered the service in the Post Office department, on May 11, 1913. In May, 1915, he qualified as clerk of the second division, subdivision B, ranking thirty-third in a competition in which there were several hundred candidates, many of whom were university graduates. In January, 1916, he was transferred to the registration branch of the Department of the Interior. In May, 1917, he -enlisted with the divisional signals and after his discharge was transferred to the dominion lands branch in 1919. In 1922 he was appointed a principal clerk as the result of a promotional -competition. In 1924 he was offered the position [DOT]of private secretary to the Minister of the Interior, who was also the minister having -charge of the administration of Indian affairs. With the exception of a few months he continued in this position until the government changed in 1930. From 1930 to 1935 he occupied the position of chief clerk in the national parks bureau. Following the change of government that year, he was brought back to the minister's office. In December, 1936, vhen the department was reorganized, Mr. Pratt was appointed to the position of assistant secretary and chief of personnel in the Department of Mines and Resources. At the same time he was appointed private secretary to the then minister and has continued to hold both positions up to the present time. It will be noted from this record that fifteen of the thirty-four years of public service were spent in work not in any way connected with the duties of a private secretary, his service in the latter capacity covering a period of nearly nineteen years.
I should like to point out that the respective ministers under whom Mr. Pratt served in the capacity of private secretary had the responsibility for the administration of Indian affairs. As private secretary during the period mentioned, he accompanied the different
;
ministers on their inspection trips throughout Canada, and in this way acquired a personal knowledge of the problems concerning the welfare of the Indians in every province. Again, as private secretary he became acquainted with the complaints made to the ministers by the Indians, and often had to discuss their grievances with them. Many of the complaints had to do with the service of the field staff, and in this way an opportunity was afforded to judge the services rendered by the personnel in the field.
As I have stated, during the last twelve years Mr. Pratt has not only acted as private secretary; he has also occupied the position of chief of personnel in the department. It can be fairly estimated that one-half his time was spent on personnel and administrative matters, and probably more than this when the house was not in session. It has been one of his duties to interview the field staff when they came to Ottawa and to discuss their problems with them. As chief of personnel it was also his duty to act as the headquarters representative on civil service boards. He also took part in the final preparation of the estimates before they were submitted to treasury board. He had to perform many other duties apart from those as private secretary, but I need not take up the time of the house in detailing them. However, it will be appreciated that his work gave him a thorough and intimate knowledge of the administration of Indian affairs, especially the problems connected with appointments and changes in staff and the expenditures required for field operations.
I think it unwise to discuss in this house the relative merits of civil servants for appointments in the service. However, the hon. member chose to do so, and- therefore I have no alternative'-and it is a privilege and pleasure for me to do so-than to speak on behalf of the civil servant whose qualifications are being belittled. I can assure hon. members that I do not look forward with any pleasure to the possibility of my secretary leaving me. On the other hand, I am not going to sit idly by and permit his qualifications for a position in the department to be questioned. I will leave it to others to judge whether his long record of public service and the experience thereby acquired does not fit him for the position to which the hon. member referred. Knowing his modest and unselfish nature, as many hon. gentlemen do, I am sure the house will accept my statement when I say that never at any time did he ask me or any other senior officer to use influence on his behalf. I know personally that he did

Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only about twelve minutes of the time of the house. My remarks will be in two sections, unless there are any interjections, in which case there may be some subsections.
The other evening, in discussing a certain tariff item, I briefly mentioned the blind, but today I should like to elaborate a little on that matter because last week was "white cane" week. The white cane is the symbol of blindness. It signifies the desire of the blind for . independence and responsibility. There are a few "do's" and "do not's" in connection with white canes; I am sure all hon. members know about them; but to refresh our memory, let me say that probably the most important "do" outside of watching carriers of white canes and being careful not to blow our horns or race our motors when stopping at stop lights if there is a white cane waiting to cross, is to remember that if you hear a white cane tapping it means the blind person wants your assistance, and you should go to him. That is probably the most important thing to remember.
Among the "do not's", after remembering not to leave tricycles, toys and children's cars on the sidewalks, probably the most important to remember is not to grasp a blind person by the arm and push him across the street. Let him take your arm; let him touch you. This is not because they are fussy but because it frustrates and excites them. They do not want anyone to push or shove them. So if you see a man with a white cane, especially if he is tapping it, just offer him your arm or coat-tail and let him tag along after you.
There are two blind organizations in Canada, which some people find confusing. There is the Canadian council of the blind, which came into being through the desire of many blind people to take an active part in the social life of their communities. Social readjustment is of vital importance to these

people. The Canadian council provides local clubs and groups so that the blind may work together in organizing their own social and recreational programs. In the council the representatives of these local groups can pool their ideas; they can have discussions and make decisions, and this is evidence that these people are capable of thinking and acting constructively and taking their part as responsible, democratic citizens. In passing, I am happy to say that the president of the Canadian council of the blind at the present time, Mrs. Sadie B. Bending, resides in London, Ontario, while the directors are scattered across the country in the various provinces.
Many are apt to confuse the Canadian council with the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. They are entirely separate organizations, though they work very closely together. The Canadian council is more or less the social, recreational and readjustment organization. The Canadian national institute is an administrative body, recognized by the governments of the dominion and the provinces as the official agency administering service to the blind and the work in connection with the prevention of blindness. This is the organization that provides teaching and educational staffs, field secretaries, librarians, departmental heads and so on to give the maximum of individual service to all registered blind people, to provide Braille and other educational facilities. At the present time they also establish refreshment booths in federal and other public buildings across the country, which afford employment for blind operators in these localities.
At the present time I believe there are about ten thousand registered blind persons across Canada, so that when we are talking about guiding allowances or additional pensions for the blind it can be seen that there is very little involved, and that no one is talking about the blind in this house for any political advantage, because there are only a few blind people in each riding. Blind1 citizens need better legislation. The Canadian council and the Canadian national institute are sponsoring a six-point program for the purpose of improving the economic welfare of the blind people of Canada. The provision of blindness allowances, which some of us call "pensions" and which is now termed "pensions", and of medical care for eye troubles is beyond the financial scope of any local organization.
The six point program of the blind: is very simple. The first is the creation of a blind persons' act entirely separate from and1 independent of the Old Age Pensions Act. The

The Address-Mr. Manross
reason for this is that for a blind person the blindness allowance is not an insurance against want in his old age, but rather a foundation or stepping stone for his future. The problems of blind people between twenty-one and seventy years of age are entirely different from those of old people over seventy who are getting the old age pension.
Then, of course, they prefer the use of the term "blindness allowance" and the elimination of the word "pension", because to them a pension means that you are pensioned off, that you are on the shelf, whereas the blindness allowance means that you are at the starting point, that you have a chance to get on in life.
Point No. 3 is that they would like the elimination of the means test, and I believe most of us will agree with that. In other words, the blind are interested in getting started. They do not think that when a blind person gets a pension at the age of twenty-one he should have to submit to the means test, because he is just getting started in life. He wants to get his education; he wants to learn Braille; he wants to learn a trade, and they believe the means test should be eliminated. After they have obtained their education or learned their craft, and have obtained employment, they want to be treated exactly the same as any other individual in Canada as far as income tax is concerned. They do not want any special treatment; but they do not believe they should have to undergo- the means test.
Point No. 4 in their program is an increase in the blindness allowance in relation to the cost of living. They believe that, having in mind the increased cost of living, $40 is not asking too much, and they hope it will be made uniform in all the provinces. We do not -think that is too much, either, because they have some expenses the ordinary person does not have.
Their next point is that under the pensions act there is a requirement that a blind person must 'be a resident of Canada for twenty years before becoming eligible for this 'blindness allowance. This is hardly fair. People have come here in good faith from other countries and, after living here for perhaps three or four or five or twelve years, have become blind through accident or some other cause and they find they can get no allowance until they have been here twenty years. They think that period- of residence should be cut to five years, and naturally I endorse that.
They also want adequate provision for medical or surgical treatment for eye conditions to conserve or to restore vision and to prevent blindness.
I felt it my duty to present this blind program because I am closely associated with their work. I know that the blind as a whole are a happy family, friendly and industrious, and are anxious to become independent. They do not like to be looked upon as being wards of the country. In my own little church at home a young blind man reads the lessons from a Braille scripture book and walks blocks in the coldest weather to help serve in his community. I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will give consideration in his estimates to helping carry out this national program for the blind, which, after all, will cost very little, and I am sure that members of all parties in the house, will be glad to approve the expenditure.

A word about my riding and the city of London. Somebody will say: Where is that? London is located half way between Toronto and Windsor on the main lines of the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway and on highway No. 2. We have also Brescia Hall, for music and theory; St. Peter's seminary and De LaSalle college, which are turning out high-class graduates; also Springbank park of 1,900 acres at the edge of the city, and Port Stanley. I want to appeal to the government, on behalf of the city of London, to unleash our business district. The city has grown, as hon. members will see from the' few industries I have mentioned, and we need a bigger and better downtown area. But the government, through no fault of their own, but caused by progress, has us fenced in. Our industries have taken over buildings. In every town there is a main corner and a street crossing it. These are considered the two main streets. So it is with London. Our business is concentrated in that small district. At the bottom of the street that runs north and south, two blocks from the main comer in the city, is the subway of the Canadian National Railways. Half a block north of the main comer there is the naval training station and an old post office which is falling down, and an old customs house across the street wdiich is being used by different departments. On the other corner there is a dominion public

building. If you walk two blocks you will find a lot of government buildings. Going west from the main corner for two blocks, you run into the river and the jail. Nobody wants to go that way. Going east, we have a fine wide street. It was widened a few years ago. Two blocks from the main comer you find the armouries. The armouries take up three-quarters of a block.
What we are asking the government to do is this. Dispose of some of these government buildings. Now is the time to dispose of property. We held an auction just recently on a small building. It is quite a long time since we listened to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I was accorded the honour of seconding the address on one occasion back in 1938, and I considered it a considerable task for a new member to be pushed into that position on his first visit. Like many other hon. members, I must congratulate the mover and the seconder on the creditable job they accomplished at that time.
My object in speaking on this occasion is not to utter a word of complaint or to make a request. I have no complaints to offer and no requests to make. I have not even any advice to offer. I am going to talk about some of the recent high spots of progress which have taken place in the riding of Renfrew North. I am not going to attempt to go into any detail with regard to my riding, but I will give the house a bird's-eye view of what has happened there recently in the way of progress. Perhaps what keeps communities content and happy is the organization of community groups. We are fairly well established in that respect. In our farming communities we have the federation of agriculture. We have credit unions, women's institutes and co-operatives. Recently we had organized in Pembroke a branch of the Women's Canadian club; a little less recently a Rotary club was organized in the little village of Douglas, and not quite so recently a branch of Rotary and a branch of the Canadian Legion was organized in the village" of Eganville.	Of course, in a town like
Pembroke we have had for many years such institutions as the Kiwanis, Rotary, Kinsmen and numerous others. Then we have the Catholic Women's League, the Alexander club, and many other organizations. In my opinion these organized groups, and others such as the board of trade, are always taking an interest in the welfare of the community in which they are established, and they have a great deal to do with the maintenance of law and order. They have a great deal to do with raising the morale and the standard of living in the different communities.
No doubt all hon. members have heard of a new place called "Deep River". Deep River gets its name from the depth of the water in that part of the Ottawa river. I do not know whether it is true or not, but it has been said that the water was so deep in that part of the river that no person had been able to sound its depth. Not so long ago things began to happen at Deep River. There was a great deal of guessing and wonderment as
The Address-Mr. Warren

to what was occurring when it was learned that a great construction operation was under way. In the course of time not only was there a huge plant constructed a few miles outside the village of Chalk River, but in addition a splendid modern little city began to take shape to house the workers and employees at Deep River. There are about two thousand people living in that modern little city. These people have all the conveniences that one could get in any city. There is a large hotel, a coffee shop, drugstores, places of worship, and so forth. There are also organized groups in the little city. To my way of thinking, it is one of the cleanest and most up-to-date little cities that one could find anywhere in Canada. If you wander around that place and have occasion to meet groups of men you learn that you have to address every second or third man by the title "doctor". I do not mean medical doctor. We have four medical doctors there, a supply of nurses and a good hospital. The doctors to whom I refer are doctors of science or doctors of something or other. One cannot help but be impressed with the fact that with so many highly qualified officials working in the laboratories of the national research council something must be taking place in that little city which will be to the benefit not only of the people of Canada but to the world as well.
If you go south from the village of Cobden a few miles you come to the village of Haley, and a couple of miles east of that village you come to another new station that has grown up within the last few years. At that plant the manufacture of a mineral or metal known as magnesium is being carried on. That site was selected because there is an inexhaustible supply of rock there easily obtainable which is suitable for the purpose for which it is required.
It is claimed that magnesium is 25 per cent lighter than aluminum and 75 per cent stronger than steel. It is a recent development, and no doubt in the course of time that metal will be turned to many thousands of uses not only in Canada but throughout the world. There is a fine modern community around that plant. The officials have all their necessary modern accommodations, and at the plant itself there is a splendid eating place with sleeping quarters for the employees.
Speaking of that particular plant, a gentleman said to me the other day that some day that place will be the Pittsburgh of Canada. The Ottawa river serves as the boundary for the riding of North Renfrew. We all know the deplorable shortage of electrical power; and it is some comfort to realize that at the

Chenaux rapids close to Portage du Fort on the Ottawa river, which is a few miles south of the village of Forester's Falls, a few miles northeast from the magnesium plant, preparations are now going on to develop power there and when completed it will produce 160,000 horsepower. If you go farther west you will find yourself still in North Renfrew when you reach Des Joachims. Work has been going on there for a considerable length of time in the development of power and, when completed, there will be a production of 480,000 horsepower. That development approximates the development at Queenston on Niagara falls. Their nominal output is 500,000 horsepower, and when this development I speak of is completed it will produce, as I have said,
480.000	horsepower.
This required the clearing of 11,000 acres of land to make way for the backing up of the Ottawa river. The water on the Ottawa river will be backed up fifty-seven miles and will require the replacement or the moving of twenty-two miles of Canadian Pacific railway and twelve miles of highway No. 17. It is estimated that it will require the removal of
2.600.000	yards of solid rock, and to accomplish this there will be needed 3,000,000 pounds of dynamite.
Just now there are 1,250 men employed on the Ontario side of the development, and they also have their own modern community, their own hospital, their own recreation halls, and an excellent eating establishment. In fact, in that particular cafeteria there is a sign reading, "If you need more good food all you have to do is to ask for it". That is in North Renfrew. These are some of the highlights of the development, and the progress which is taking place in North Renfrew, and which I think should be generally known.
Hon. members know, of course, about Petawawa military camp. That camp is being transformed into a permanent military camp.
I believe that Petawawa military camp is recognized as probably the best, training centre in the world for artillery purposes. I do not think there is any better spot for the training of bridge builders. In my opinion Canadian artillerymen trained at Petawawa were unsurpassed during world war I and the last world war. I was interested to watch the training of those men in bridge building and later on to learn, when they came home, that many of them had been taken from Canadian corps and placed with other regiments of the British armies because of their expert knowledge of bridge building. During the last war they built bridges all over Europe, including the bridge across the Rhine.

The Address-Mr. Warren
The Petawawa military camp comprises 131 square miles, A part of that military ground, covering 95 square miles, was taken over in 1923 by the Department of Mines and Resources and it is used as an experimental forestry station. Too few of us know of the splendid work that is being carried on at that station. That work is of very great value. Experiments of all sorts are being carried on there, for example, in connection with the protection of undergrowth, the best methods to use in thinning the forest, or the proper distances to leave between trees so as to promote the best growth. There is also work in connection with fire protection and the study of insect [DOT]diseases such as the spruce budworm, the white pine weevil, the heart rot in poplar, and white pine blister. If such diseases can be overcome we shall have accomnlished a great deal in forest protection not only in Ontario but throughout the Dominion of Canada.
Speaking of that area of 95 square miles, [DOT]during the war years an internment camp was erected at Centre lake. I think I am safe in saying that of all of the thousands of prisoners interned in that camp, not one who escaped was not returned in a short time to the camp. Of course a good deal of credit must go to the veterans of world war I who served as a security guard at the camp.
It was an ideal place for an internment camp. These prisoners of war cut their own wood for fuel; they did their own cooking; they looked after their own affairs, and besides that they helped to build roads and in a general way were kept busy. That, I think, was a good thing. At the forestry station, there is a nice community, proper sleeping quarters, and eating places and homes for the officials. A great many conscientious objectors were taken care of there, and much useful work done during their term. It is interesting to note that during the years sixty miles of road have been built through that forest, thirty miles of telephone line and two lookout towers, besides many bridges. But it would be a mistake to think all of that land was going to waste or was not in production during peacetime, because this timber was always growing. Every year a great deal of timber is sold to contractors. Of course any timber that is sold from there must be taken out under the supervision of the forestry officials who mark the trees which they will permit to be cut. Needless to say, all brush and slash must be burned at the time of cutting.
In Renfrew North we have types of soils ranging from heavy clay to light sand. In Petawawa township we have a type of sand suitable for the cultivation of tobacco and
some day we may compete with Norfolk county in tobacco growing. In fact. Major Forgie of the town of Pembroke, who has been doing some experimental work, is fairly well convinced that some day we shall be producing tobacco on an unlimited amount of land in Petawawa township. In 1947 the farmers on the heavier lands were not quite so fortunate as those on the lighter soils. The farmers on the lighter soils in at least some cases had good grain crops, whereas many farmers on the heavier soils, as a result of the wet spring, did not. But if we lose one crop in Renfrew county we are not likely to starve. Every farmer, whether on heavy soil or on light soil, had a wonderful crop of hay. This year any farmer who did not want to feed his hay on his own farm had available a ready market at a fine price.
We grow a great deal of alfalfa. We have hammer mills which transform this alfalfa hay into a meal which is shipped all over the country and exported. It is one of the necessary ingredients of poultry feed, feed for young hogs and dairy feeds. As a matter of fact. I should not be surprised if some of it went as far as Fraser Valley.

These women, after careful study, have become expert in the handling of poultry and eggs. In Renfrew North this business has become big business. It is interesting also to note that in Renfrew county there was a substantial increase in hogs in 1947 over 1946, a substantial increase in the output of butter in 1947 over 1946, and a substantial increase in the revenue from beef production over 1946. If everything else fails, we always have something to fall back on. We have logging. In almost any community you can mention you will find a sawmill. I often wonder where the logs come from, but they keep coming. This year you may think there will not be any
The Arid reus-Mr. Macdonnell

next year, but next year you find that there are just as many. Something that we sometimes lose sight of is the fact that trees keep on growing. The logging industry in. Renfrew North is a wonderful sideline, not only for many farmers, but for jobbers and contractors as well. There is a market for such timber as poplar. We have such plants as the Pembroke Shook Mills in Pembroke and the Canadian Splint and Lumber Company. The better timber is always going out to various points throughout the country.
We have the most wonderful tourist attractions that can be imagined, almost anywhere one likes to go throughout the riding of Renfrew North. We have lakes without number, plenty of fish, splendid hunting grounds, unequalled scenery, good hotels, good accommodations and good tourist resorts. I would say to hon. members that if at any time they want to have a good day they should go up highway No. 17, or go to Golden Lake, or go in any direction they may wish to throughout the riding of Renfrew North, and I feel sure they will come back happy and pleased.

I wish to spend some time this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, talking about a danger which is overhanging our country, a danger which is serious now, which could become disastrous, which I think few people correctly understand, and which, for reasons I shall try to make clear, the government seems unwilling to disclose and underline for the benefit of the public. I refer, of course, to inflation. Inflation is- a dreadful thing. I want to quote briefly from the London Economist of January 17, 1948. After speaking about the slow realization in England of what they call the suppressed inflation there, they say this:
... it is obviously true that inflation is the great problem everywhere else in the world.
Then, farther on, they say of England:
Not merely is there an obvious inflation, but it is also clearly reaching the rampant stage.
We have to remind ourselves of what lias happened elsewhere in the world. It is well to remember that inflation in Germany prepared the way for Hitler, because I suppose it is true to say it was the destruction of the middle class in Germany that eventually brought about the conditions of which Hitler took advantage. We are told that today the Russians hope inflation will win for them what they call the "cold war". In that connection it is interest-

ing to read what was said just after the last war by a great economist who became famous, the late Lord Keynes:
Lenin is said to have declared that the best way to destroy the capitalist system was to debauch the currency. By a continuing process of inflation, governments can confiscate, secretly and unobserved, an important part of the wealth of their citizens. By this method they not only confiscate, but they confiscate arbitrarily; and, while the process impoverishes many, it actually enriches some.

Whether we like it or not, we have a considerable amount of inflation in Canada today. Therefore it seems to me it is the manifest duty of the government to be impressing that upon us, to be warning us of the danger, to be calling upon us for the exercise of self-control. Instead of that, however, what do we actually find? We had a resolution introduced a few weeks ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) dealing with price spreads. Did that resolution have anything to say about inflation? I do not think the word was used in it. Three or four cabinet ministers, in addition to the Prime Minister, spoke during the debate; and while I will not undertake to say that the word "inflation" was not used by them, I will undertake to say that the point was not seriously made. I doubt very much if it was even mentioned by any of them as a prominent point. In other words, in my opinion that resolution deals entirely with results and not with causes. A witty American, writing about the witch hunt after price spreads, has said, "Inflation is the crime and the government is the criminal." What we actually find is that the government, I suppose because they have a sense of responsibility and wish to divert people's minds, had this committee appointed to deal with profits, hoarding and speculation, according to the terms of reference ; all of which I believe have trifling, microscopic effects on the present situation. In other words, what they are dealing with, as I said a moment ago, are effects, while ignoring the causes; turning away from causes and looking for scapegoats, or a kind of decoy.
How is it, Mr. Speaker, that the citizens of Canada ever allow them to get away with

The Address-Mr. Maedonnell
that? I suppose the first reason is that we in this country have never been exposed to the full blast of inflation. With us it has never been anything more than an inconvenience. We think of inflation as a thing that happens in funny foreign countries where they do not know how to look after their affairs properly. Yet people like the Germans, after the first war, were sensible people and usually able to look after their financial affairs pretty well. I consider it well to remind ourselves that before the first war we in this country used to think about war in exactly the same way. We thought war was a thing that happened in funny, far-off countries, usually inhabited bv coloured people, and we never really believed it would come to us at all.
Let us look back for a moment at this thing we call inflation. In our school books we used to read about the debasing of me currency and about kings who clipped the coinage. Well, we do not have that sort of thing today. In those days, debasing the currency was really much easier to detect. In these days, when we have paper money and the amount of money is limited only by the amount of paper produced by the mills, it is extraordinarily difficult to find out exactly what a government is doing; and, as I shall show, we have inflation now in a very substantial way. If we do not take care and take immediate steps we may have it to a very much greater degree.
The government of Canada at one time had a very sound view on the matter of inflation. I want to read a short passage from the budget speech in September, 1939, which I have no hesitation in- saying was an able document. In that speech, after pointing out that, of necessity, a certain amount of inflation I think it was in the form of borrowing from the banks-was to -be used in order to get the economy moving, because, of course, in 1939 things were pretty dull, the then minister of finance went on to say:
However, as soon as the expansion of employment and production gets well under way and certainly before it approaches its limits, further expansion of the supply of money and credit must be stopped if the danger of progressive inflation is to be avoided. With an economy at full production and employment, the only result of expanding money and credit is to raise prices without increasing production. At such a point commences the cumulative spiral of inflation with all its deadly consequences to the economy.
That wyas the view of the finance department in the autumn of 1939, and of course it is well for us to remember that was early in the war; that we could not expect to foresee the course events were taking, so that no fairminded person would object to the fact that during the war the government was not able to hold fast to that sound principle.
Well, we all know in a rough and ready way what we mean by inflation, the phrase has become current; too much money chasing too [DOT] few goods. A rather more dignified description given by an economist is this; "the situation where the flow of money incomes is greater than the goods and services available for purchase with such incomes at prevailing prices".
I have stated that there is inflation. Let us take a brief glance back now at what actually happened, and see how it arose. First of all, I want to give a few simple figures showing how money and its equivalent in terms of purchasing power have increased since 1939. Of course in that year the country was rather inactive. We should bear that in mind in making a comparison with 1939; otherwise we may reach an extreme view, and I have no desire to do that. The question is far too serious for anyone to want to exaggerate. Here are the facts. In 1939 the money in people's pockets, let us call it money in the till, money in the heel of the sock, or anything of that sort, amounted1 to $216 million. It is now a billion dollars, or multiplied almost five times. Savings deposits, which, of course, are also a means of payment, were then $1 billion. They have now increased to $3,800 million. Demand deposits in 1939 amounted -to $800 million. They are now $1,300 million. In other words, the total of these three in 1939 was $2,100 million, and in 1947, $7,100 million; and as a matter of fact I have seen since then a somewhat larger figure.
You may ask whether I am suggesting that, because the quantity of money is up three times, therefore prices should be multiplied by three. No, it is not as simple as that; it is not a question in simple arithmetic. Nevertheless every serious student of money and the effect of money agrees that the quantity of purchasing power available has a profound effect, and- therefore I wish to talk more about it.
By the way, a moment ago I omitted to say that in addition to the increase of from $2,100 million in 1939 to $7,100 million in 1947 there are also in the hands of the public $6,000 million in victory bonds, which, as anyone will see, really are a means of payment, readily available.
I should like also to say I think it was desirable that there should have been some rise in price from 1939. It is hard to say
The Address-Mr. Macdonnell

what would have been the ideal place at which to stop, but it is suggested that perhaps 1940 or 1941, or somewhere about the time when controls w'ere ,put on would have been a proper time. That is a matter of opinion, and I am not committing myself. But, as I say, I believe we should not regard the situation in 1939 as ideal.
Now', how did that arise? The situation is very simple, as you look back. I read a minute ago the fine intentions as set out in the budget of 1939, that as soon as they got the wheels of industry turning further inflation should stop. But of course that was 1939, and we did not foresee the years from 1940 to 1945.
In those years what happened? We all remember that, because of the war, we got many billions of dollars. You all remember that we paid half of it out of taxation, and for that I give the finance department full credit. I think the way they put taxes on was to their credit. But of the balance, some four billions of dollars was raised by borrowing from the banking system; that is where the real inflation came in. And, again, I am not criticizing what was done during the war. It was what was done after the war that I am criticizing.
Anyway let us see what did happen. That four billions of dollars was borrowed; you get it in the figures I read to you. What did we get in exchange? Well, we got those things that the then minister of munitions and supply was turning out in profusion. We got aeroplanes and ships and guns and shells and munitions; we paid the armed forces; and we built factories.
Then, at the end of the war, in exchange for all that huge amount of money poured out, what did we have? The aeroplanes and the ships were practically worthless. We sold them for a song, if indeed they were still in existence. The shells had been used; the munitions had been fired; the guns had been fired. That was at the end of the war when we had a situation where very little was left, represented by that four billion dollars worth of purchasing power, with the addition of six billions in bonds.
I do not think any fair-minded man up to that time had any complaints about what
was happening. We knew it had to be done, and we all applauded the then minister of munitions and supply. He w'ent ahead and did it; he got the munitions of war, and we did not worry much about the cost. We wanted to win the war.
Then we came to the end of the rvar. There we were-and we were bursting with money, and at the same time short of all kinds of goods. We were short of houses, motorcars and all kinds of household goods which I need not take time to mention. In a word, there was practically an unlimited demand for goods. People's pockets were bursting with money, and we were in very short supply. In other words, one might say that we had material lying around for a prairie fire. What I complain about

and here is where my complaint begins, namely in 1945-is that, instead of damping down this fire, from that time on-and it is still continuing-the government have, in my opinion, added fuel to the flames. And that is very largely the reason we find ourselves in this situation today.
Why did they do that? As will be seen from the white paper of employment and income issued in 1945, they thought-and-I do not think anyone blamed them at that time- that there would probably be a recession. They thought that all the devices which had been used in war would have to be carried forward into peace, and that we would have to have an easy-money policy to stimulate imports. If we read that white paper of the spring of 1945 we see that all the techniques which had been used in war for stimulating the raising of money and keeping exchange rates low' were all outlined, in effect, in that memorandum, as. something that would continue.
